title: Wilson Survey Signals Need for New Understanding of Verification Success
gist: The Siemens-sponsored Wilson functional verification survey shows first-silicon success falling to 5% from a roughly 30% decade-long average. Siemens' Harry Foster attributes the drop to five factors including AI accelerator complexity, hardware-software coupling, and growth in firmware, safety and security respins.

insights.claim: Functional verification survey data show the share of designs claiming first-silicon success has fallen to 5% in the latest survey, from an average of roughly 30% over at least a decade.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Rising respin risk raises chip cost and time-to-market risk, favouring verification spend and emulation.
insights.locator: Where an average of ~30% of designs claimed first silicon success

insights.claim: Silicon respins are expensive and risk missing market windows, so the discipline has been to maximize coverage pre-silicon, yet teams are still falling behind despite more people, compute, abstraction and AI-based methods.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Verification capacity lags design complexity growth.

insights.claim: AI/GPU and CPU cluster designs have coherency issues (cache and IO), amplified by memory shared across data collection, feature extraction, inference and working memory, that may not surface for billions of cycles but are as fatal to a launch as easily caught bugs.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Deep bugs in AI silicon raise respin risk for accelerator programmes.

insights.claim: AI architectures have become fundamentally more complex to manage PPA tradeoffs for billion-plus parameter models at competitive inference response times and acceptable power budgets.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Design difficulty is a barrier to entry for AI chip competitors.

insights.claim: The line between hardware and software functionality has blurred through controllers in secure boot and safety IP, mixed ISAs with custom extensions, and AI engines with specialized datatypes, making verification against representative workloads much harder.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Pre-silicon verification increasingly needs software-stack scale, favouring large emulation platforms.
insights.locator: Software is intimately linked to hardware

insights.claim: Synthetic tests, system-level VIP, PSS, emulation and FPGA prototyping are only partial answers: they cannot verify far up the software stack except on the largest hardware accelerators, and running large models may induce races, lockups or errors that cannot be detected pre-silicon.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Limits of current EDA verification tools leave an opening for new methods and post-silicon validation.

insights.claim: SystemVerilog, once dominant for UVM testbenches, is now neck and neck with C/C++ and Python, while PSS is growing fast from behind; Foster reads this as teams responding to complexity rather than a cause of low success rates.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Tool-vendor exposure shifts toward software-style and abstraction-level verification.

insights.claim: The survey showed significant growth in respins tied to firmware, safety and security, where secure control, software-stack interaction and telemetry make high coverage of possible threats hard.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Security and safety IP verification is a growing respin driver.

insights.claim: The verification problem space is now much bigger than the old view that a chip meeting spec is done, which the author takes as a sign more creative verification approaches are coming.
insights.speaker: Bernard Murphy
insights.so_what: Expect continued investment and product launches in verification.
